messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: If some sub-group are not normal distribution,can I use multipleGroup()?
parts:
IRT makes no assumptions about the distribution of total scores, only the latent trait distribution and functional forms for each item. What you are observing here is not relevant as to whether a multiple-group model is reasonable or not (it would be though if you were using CTT analyses).

Phil

messages.subject: Re: If some sub-group are not normal distribution,can I use multipleGroup()?
parts:
On Thu, Jul 16, 2020 at 6:33 PM Stan Silver <mailtoy...@gmail.com> wrote:
Totally agree with your `The distribution of sum scores is not synonymous with the distribution of the latent traits`.  But they are highly correlated.

I'm still not sure why exactly you believe this to be true, but it's demonstrably false. For instance, you can have a strong positive skewness in the sum-scores and yet the latent trait scores are genuinely normal. See the code and figures below. This is why I'm still not sure why you think your latent traits are non-normal based only on total score information.

library(mirt)
set.seed(1234)
a <- rlnorm(50, .2, .2)
d <- -rlnorm(50, .2, .4)
theta <- matrix(rnorm(5000))

dat <- simdata(a, d, itemtype = '2PL', Theta=theta)
hist(rowSums(dat), 20, main = 'Histogram of total scores')

mod <- mirt(dat, 1)
coef(mod, simplify=TRUE)
fs <- fscores(mod, method = 'plausible')
hist(fs, 30, main = 'Histogram of plausible latent trait estimates')
If sub-groups' latent distribution is not normal,can I still use `dentype = "Gaussian"`? If not,what  alternative dentype can use?

If you must, and believe that your latent traits are indeed non-normal, you could try to fit mixture or Davidian curves as potential semi-parametric smoothing solutions. Or, if you have a more specific distributional form, simply write your own using createGroup() as I've stated in previous posts.

Phil

Thanks in advance.

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: If some sub-group are not normal distribution,can I use multipleGroup()?
parts:
If you're not sure of the latent trait distribution then I'm not sure it makes sense to play around with different prior distributions. Just treat the latent trait distribution as an initial prior, where you know the results could be biased (this is a typical Bayesian mentality). You could use fscores() to approximate some distribution after the fact, but again this is only approximate since a) the model is likely biased from choosing an incorrect latent trait distribution prior, and b) the prior used in many  the point-wise computations of the latent traits is also likely incorrect, leading to a double amount of noise. Latent traits are tricky at times, and two-step approaches are not perfect.

Phil
